summary: A tool was developed for scientists, engineers, space agencies, and the general public interested in planning lunar landings at any point on the Moon’s surface, taking into account the ephemerides between the Moon, the Earth, and the Sun. These data make it possible to know the relative position of the three bodies precisely and, with it, the lighting conditions and geometry that directly affect a mission’s feasibility. To address this challenge, the team designed a web application with a backend built in Python with FastAPI, responsible for processing and exposing the data, and a frontend developed in TypeScript with React, which offers an interactive and easy-to-use interface. The tool also integrates the NASA (JPL) Horizons System API to obtain the ephemerides, and digital elevation models (DEMs) from the LOLA instrument, which describe the lunar terrain in great detail. This initiative could make lunar landing mission planning easier by identifying viable sites and avoiding the critical areas of the lunar surface, such as steep slopes, craters, or areas with unfavorable conditions. In this way, it helps reduce risks, optimize the selection of landing sites, and bring lunar exploration to a wider audience.
details: The tool has a backend built with Python and FastAPI, which makes calls to the Horizons System API and retrieves the LOLA elevation maps, processed with Rasterio. The tool allows users to intuitively visualize landing sites and details of the selected area, enabling a better view of the zone to understand how viable a landing could be. It is expected to have a beneficial impact on future research carried out on the Moon, as well as on space agencies, planning, and logistics. The frontend was developed with TypeScript and React, using HTML and CSS to structure the content, and Visual Studio Code was used as the code editor. Its creativity lies in the way it presents information: through 3D models of the Moon and the representation of its surface with Three.js, along with representations of the Earth and the Sun from the Moon’s point of view, and 2D representations for the maps of the north and south poles and the equatorial plane. The factors taken into account in developing the digital tool were the following: research, the terrain along with the Moon’s ephemerides, the positions of the Sun and the Earth, the periods of solar illumination, the windows of direct communication with the Earth, and simple feasibility analyses of the selected site.
dataRefs: NASA Identifies Candidate Regions for Landing Next Americans on Moon
